title: The database's shape
headline: The database's shape is sound for a platform about to open: dead objects are rare (1 table, 5 columns, 34 leftover tables), triggers are gated by column and nearly every log has a retention rule; that 245 of 486 tables have held no row says only that the doors are still closed, and nothing is retired for it. What is worth fixing before opening is where cost does not follow use or grows with stores: pg_cron's run log is 564 MB of the 731 MB database and nothing prunes it, every cold start evaluates a 1 MB schema file that no query uses (115 to 135 ms and 9 to 12 MB measured), 122 store filters are written so the store index cannot serve them, and page lists read whole documents (4.2 ms a call against 0.8 ms from a plain column, measured in a local Postgres 18). All 14 verified findings now have ordered steps, the tests and rules that hold them and one check; one was added: indexes are declared in two places and nothing compares them, which is how two of the three duplicates on orders and order_lines arrived. Do first DS-8 (the scheduler's log), DS-1 (the schema import), DS-7 (the store filter) and DS-15 with DS-9 (the duplicate-index test and the 13 drops); DS-6 (the platform kept twice) and DS-13's retention periods wait for the owner.

findings.title: pg_cron's run log is 564 MB of the 731 MB database and nothing prunes it
findings.evidence: The statistics give 731 MB for the database: the cron schema 564 MB, commerce 124 MB. pg_cron writes one row to cron.job_run_details per run with the whole command text. The baseline schedules 9 jobs a minute, 1 every five minutes and 4 daily (baseline_4:93-113, which I read): 13,252 rows a day. Two of the daily jobs are retention deletes (consents, cookie_scans); none prunes the run log. rg for job_run_details over src, scripts and supabase finds nothing.
findings.cost: Measured: 564 MB, 77% of the database. Estimate: about 8 MB more a day at today's schedule (13,252 rows of about 0.6 KB), about 3 GB a year, whatever the number of stores. Larger backups, slower restores and branches.
fix_steps: 1. Before writing the file, read two facts on production (one read-only statement through the Supabase tool): select has_table_privilege('postgres', 'cron.job_run_details', 'TRUNCATE') as may_truncate, count(*) as rows, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('cron.job_run_details')) as size from cron.job_run_details.

2. Make a custom migration: pnpm exec drizzle-kit generate --custom --name cron_run_log_retention, then node scripts/prune-snapshots.mjs. Its body is one DO block that does nothing where the cron schema is missing (the tests' PGlite and CI's Postgres have none): IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = 'cron') THEN … END IF.

3. Inside the block, empty the log once: IF has_table_privilege(current_user, 'cron.job_run_details', 'TRUNCATE') THEN TRUNCATE cron.job_run_details; ELSE DELETE FROM cron.job_run_details WHERE end_time < now() - interval '7 days'; END IF. TRUNCATE gives the space back at once; a DELETE only lets it be reused. The app never reads this log (its own ledger is commerce.cron_jobs).

4. In the same block schedule the standing prune, as the two retention jobs at baseline_4:105-113 are scheduled: PERFORM cron.schedule('kaizen-cron-log-retention', '41 3 * * *', $job$ DELETE FROM cron.job_run_details WHERE end_time < now() - interval '7 days' $job$). cron.schedule with a name replaces the job of that name, so the file can run again.

5. Do not edit baseline_4 (D572: a baseline is never edited). At the next quarterly squash, scripts/squash-migrations.mjs lists files with a scheduler step: fold this job into the new baseline_4 by hand (docs/ci-migrations.md:46).
6. Push the file; CI's release job applies it. Then check the advisors and record the file's version in docs/decisions.md under Migration versions.
7. If step 3 could only delete and the 564 MB matter (backups, branches), ask for one VACUUM FULL cron.job_run_details from a role that owns the table; otherwise leave it: the file stops growing.

findings.title: Indexes are declared in two places and nothing compares them, which is how duplicates reached orders and order_lines
findings.evidence: An index is made either in src/db/schema.ts (drizzle writes the migration) or by hand in a custom migration, as the rule for hot tables requires for a concurrent build (docs/ci-migrations.md:60-62). pnpm db:check compares schema.ts with drizzle's own snapshot, so a hand-written index is invisible to it. On the migrated test database 46 of the 1,059 non-unique indexes are named nowhere in schema.ts, 12 of them on hot tables. Two of those 12 are twins of a declared index: orders_invoice_candidates_idx (baseline_3:10328) has the key of orders_store_placed_idx (schema.ts:4899), and order_lines_analytics_idx (baseline_3:10062) has the key of order_lines_order_idx (schema.ts:5092, baseline_3:10076). No test looks for an index led by another: a catalog query I ran on the test database finds 11 such plain indexes today.
findings.cost: No direct cost. Each duplicate that slips in is one more index entry on every write of its table, and the hot tables are where hand-written indexes are made.
findings.who_pays: The database per write, later; CI
fix_steps: 1. Add src/db/index-duplicates.test.ts, using createTestDatabase() from src/db/testing.ts like the other src/db tests. It runs one catalog query: for btree indexes of schema commerce, list each plain (not unique) index A whose key columns, taken with pg_get_indexdef(indexrelid, k, true) for k in 1..indnkeyatts, equal the leading columns of another index B on the same table, where B is longer, or unique, or A's name sorts after B's. The working query is in the scratch file named in notes.

findings.title: Ending one sandbox runs at least 800 deletes and holds about 2,100 locks, one pass per store table per round
findings.evidence: purge_sandbox() loops over every commerce table with a store_id column but two and runs a dynamic DELETE in its own exception block, and repeats the whole pass until a pass deletes nothing (baseline_1:15393-15417): at least two passes. On the real schema that is 400 tables. I ran the function's own loop in PGlite for a store id that owns nothing: one pass is 400 statements, took 64 to 293 ms (the first run, with cold caches, the longest), and left 2,129 relation locks held by the transaction, because planning each delete locks the table and all its indexes. It is the only function in the baseline that builds statements from the catalog. purgeSandboxes() takes up to 25 sandboxes a run, one after the other (sandbox.ts:369-380).
findings.cost: Estimate: 0.1 to 0.5 s of database time per ended sandbox. Measured: about 2,100 lock entries held until commit, which is a third of a default Postgres lock table (64 a connection, 100 connections). Both rise with every table and index added, not with what the sandbox held. The cost follows use, one visitor's try of the builder.
fix_steps: 1. Small step, now: a custom migration that replaces commerce.purge_sandbox() with the same body and one new first statement, PERFORM pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('commerce.purge_sandbox')), so two purges never hold their locks at the same time (two dispatcher runs can overlap).
2. Read production's limits once (show max_locks_per_transaction; show max_connections) and write them in docs/builder-sandbox.md beside the measured 2,129 locks a purge holds.

3. Only if those limits leave less than about four times a purge's locks, or sandboxes are purged by the hundred a day: split the work. A new function commerce.purge_sandbox_part(p_sandbox uuid, p_after text, p_tables integer default 50) deletes from the next 50 store tables and returns the last name; purgeSandbox() in src/server/sandbox.ts:365 calls it in a loop, each call its own transaction, in rounds until a full round deletes nothing; a last function then writes the tombstone and the sandbox's state as lines 15418-15422 do. No transaction then holds more than about 300 locks.
4. Whatever is done, keep the guarantee: the purge refuses any store that is not a closed sandbox whose row is expired, and ends only when a full pass deletes nothing.
tests_and_rules: src/db/sandboxes.test.ts:313-327 and :406 (the purge refuses any other store; it returns the rows deleted) and src/server/sandbox.int.test.ts (files first, then rows): must pass unchanged after step 1.
src/server/sandbox.int.test.ts runs on a real Postgres: add a case that two purges started together both finish, one after the other.
Rule: docs/builder-sandbox.md:214-222 (what purge_sandbox() refuses and that it deletes every row of the store).
findings.done_when: src/server/sandbox.int.test.ts has a case where two purges started together both finish, and docs/builder-sandbox.md states production's max_locks_per_transaction and max_connections beside the 2,129 locks one purge holds.
findings.saving: No time saved by step 1; it removes the case of two purges holding about 4,300 lock entries together. Step 3, if ever needed: from about 2,100 locks in one transaction to about 300.
findings.risk: Low for step 1. Medium for step 3: the function is the guarantee that nothing of a sandbox is left, so the split must end with a pass that finds nothing.
findings.notes: Not worth more than step 1 now: the cost follows use, is a fraction of a second, and one purge fits a default lock table. The verified report's fix (ask first which tables hold a row) would not lower the lock count: the asking locks the same tables and indexes. DS-12's count will show this cost growing with the schema.
